newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Coffee gets dizzy, then finds buying.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee gets dizzy, then finds buying.

text.p: World coffee prices dropped on Tuesday but found buying at weaker values to suggest that the supply worries and speculative interest that have lifted them by some 50 percent this year had yet to go away.

Arabica coffee futures traded in the New York market have set the pace in the rally that has been based on a perception that stocks are low and that Brazil may have a smaller crop, as well as labour unrest in Colombia.
The rally has led to rises in retail prices on ground coffee in Europe and the United States.

When New York reopened after the long President's Day weekend on Tuesday the most active May arabica contract was soon down to a low at 154 cents per pound, down 13 cents, but it recovered by around midday to trade above 163 cents.
Speculative liquidation battered the early market on news that Colombian union leaders and government officials reached a deal early Tuesday to end an eight-day strike by state workers.

London futures for the lower quality Robusta type of coffee rose as high as $1,705 per tonne on Friday ended Tuesday down at $1,560 on hedge selling and speculative liquidation. But trade buying had lifted them off the day's low at $1,550.

World oil prices, extending a sell-off of nearly 15 percent in the last month, fell to their lowest since last August at just above $20 for a barrel of North Sea Brent Blend crude, as warm weather on both sides of the Atlantic highlighted a growing supply picture.
But prices steadied and some analysts felt the recent sell-off was near an end.
"The fact that it is so oversold tells me that you don't want to sell down here," cautioned Tom Bentz, a vice president at ING in New York.
Copper prices ended modestly firmer, joined by most of the other London Metal Exchange (LME) base metals. Widening backwardation in the copper market was the main feature in otherwise thin trading.
Three months delivery copper ended the afternoon session at $2,286 per tonne, up a modest $8 from Monday.
But the cash to threes backwardation -- the premium for cash over three-months delivery -- flared out after starting at around $60 in the morning and ended the kerb at $72/$82.
The widening spreads, indicating tight nearby supply, along with a small drawdown in stocks provided support for copper.
"There is still a great deal of nervousness ...stocks are relatively low and vulnerable. Nobody wants to be short in case tightness reappears," a trader said.
On a fundamental level, traders were watching for a spike in Chinese demand for base metals. But so far any sizable Chinese business was absent from the market, traders said.
Aluminium, helped by a 5,050-tonne decline in stocks, ended at its highs and $14 firmer at $1,584 per tonne.
Mining companies should be cautious of building new copper mines since an era of high prices seems to be ending, a report by industrial consultant CRU International said.

"With the current run of high copper prices likely to be nearing its end, mining companies and financiers need to look very carefully at the economic and technical viability of the projects they are involved in," CRU said.
The CRU report examined 20 projects which could account for almost three million tonnes of new copper production per year with total capital expenditure in excess of $13 billion.
"Only five of the 20 major projects examined can be categorised as sure-fire winners," it added.

CRU rates the Voisey's Bay project in Canada, where copper is a by-product of nickel, as the most viable project. The second most attractive and the biggest is Collahuasi in Chile, in which Canada's Falconbridge Ltd has a 44 percent interest.

US grains prices were modestly firmer with Chicago wheat futures up five cents around $3.65 per bushel, mainly on export news and fund buying. Gold had a London afternoon fixing at $345 an ounce, up 90 cents from Monday, but bullion markets saw little drama.
